#6633. New York City’s Toughest Tables to Book This Holiday Season

Scoring a difficult reservation feels that much sweeter this time of year.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The holidays in New York are when the city feels most alive. Fifth Avenue’s shop windows glitter, hotel lobbies become elaborate seasonal spectacles, and the dining rooms that anchor the city’s social scene take on an added measure of importance. From Thanksgiving through New Year’s Eve, securing a table at the right restaurant can be as much a part of the holiday as seeing the tree at Rockefeller Center. The most coveted rooms are filled with out-of-towners, old friends back in the city, and New Yorkers determined to make the most of the season. Here are some of the toughest, most in-demand tables to book in New York this time of year—and the reservations worth pursuing for serious bragging rights to round out your 2026.

This reservation is coveted all year round, but the exclusivity of this fantastic restaurant takes on added coziness and flair come the holidays. Its wood-paneled dining room, equestrian memorabilia, and old-school American menu have made it a lasting favorite of the city’s well-heeled diners. You have to call the number on its website. May the odds be ever in your favor.

For a holiday evening that feels atmospheric and old-school, head to The Jazz Club at Aman New York. Tucked beneath the hotel, this intimate venue pairs live jazz with a sophisticated setting. Between the limited seating and the appeal of an evening at one of Manhattan’s most in-demand luxury hotels, advance planning is essential. New Year’s Eve will be especially enviable to book—there will be live music and a countdown.

Since opening in 2024, The Corner Store has been one of downtown’s most talked-about restaurants, in no small part due to a succession of visits from recurring customer Taylor Swift. A reservation here carries social currency, especially during the holidays—last year, during Hanukkah, The Corner Store offered a viral Matzo Ball Martini. Keep an eye out for more fun seasonal specials this year.

Watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade from four floors above Columbus Circle at an iconic, Michelin-starred restaurant? Say less. Per Se hosts a special Thanksgiving brunch with front-row views of the parade balloons, alongside chef-curated tasting stations featuring turkey, caviar, Island Creek Oysters, lobster rolls, and more. There’s also balloon twisting and face painting for the kids. There are a few reservations still available through Tock.

Thanksgiving at The Nines is a glamorous alternative to the typical family gathering. The restaurant serves a prix fixe holiday dinner featuring traditional dishes alongside its own signature offerings, with live piano music to boot. The 2026 seating is currently sold out, but Resy offers the option to receive an alert should a table become available.

A reservation at 4 Charles Prime Rib is difficult any time of year, but this West Village townhouse restaurant becomes particularly appealing this time of year. Known for its intimate, clubby atmosphere and indulgent steakhouse fare, 4 Charles releases its reservations 21 days in advance, and they always seem to disappear within seconds. If all else fails, it’s offering At Home Packages for Thanksgiving, so you can enjoy its all-American cuisine without having to jockey for a table.

L’Artusi has been a West Village fixture for two decades, and its popularity shows little sign of waning. During the winter months, the restaurant leans into the season with festive décor, winter truffle dishes, and rotating chef’s specials that celebrate the season. Its relatively small dining room means tables are always in demand. There is good news for devotees, however: A second, larger location is slated to open in Rockefeller Center this spring.

Few New York restaurants commit to the holiday bit like Rolf’s—a Gramercy institution that is known for its ceilings festooned with thousands of Christmas ornaments, twinkling lights, and garlands. The décor stays up all year round, but the holiday period is especially competitive to score reservations. You have to call to book. Good luck.

For those spending Christmas Eve in Manhattan, Chez Fifi offers a distinctly French alternative to your typical holiday dinner. The Upper East Side restaurant—known as one of the neighborhood’s hottest tables to book right now—offers French-Basque specialties, from steak au poivre to roasted chicken and baba au rhum, alongside foie gras terrine and seasonal specials. Pro tip for those having trouble scoring a reservation: the restaurant holds some upstairs seating for release the day before.

West Village hot spot Galo is a new addition to the restaurant scene but has become a quick favorite for in-the-know diners. Housed in a historic carriage house on West 10th Street, it’s about as cozy as you can get—and is one of the few popular restaurants of its ilk to be open on Christmas Day. An ode to the chef’s native Portugal, the menu spans large-format heritage dishes and shareable petiscos, like bacalhau, wine-poached pears, and a variety of special port wines.

Housed in a historic Rockefeller Center townhouse once frequented by Johnny Carson and generations of Saturday Night Live cast members, Pebble Bar oozes authentic New York history. Its intimate dining room is particularly appealing during the holidays, thanks to its proximity to the Rockefeller Center tree, Radio City Music Hall, and Fifth Avenue’s windows. With just nine dining tables, availability is limited—but the restaurant does reserve some space for walk-ins, so a spontaneous drop-in might work out in your favor.

Few dining rooms offer a better vantage point for the holiday season than L’Avenue at Saks, perched on the ninth floor of the iconic Fifth Avenue department store. Its seasonal Le Chalet experience adds live piano, festive cocktails—including a must-try French Onion Martini—and views of the Rockefeller Center tree to the equation. Reservations go quickly in the month of December, when the restaurant can serve 600 to 800 guests a day. Reservations are available through Resy.

#6632. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. Garfield’s forthcoming Artificial (out December 25) is the movie on everybody’s lips, but he told me he’s looking forward to spending the holidays in New York and taking a brief break before what will probably be a busy campaign season for the Man of the Year.

No one captured the evening as succinctly as Robby Hoffman, who described her upcoming TV show as “Curb [Your Enthusiasm] for poor people.” When the conversation turned back to GQ, Hoffman rued the decline of magazine paper quality. But this latest issue got her seal of approval: appropriately glossy, well-considered, and elite to the touch. Though she might have just been describing the party’s guest list.

But even if you didn’t make the cut, you can see how GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party looked from the inside. ✦

#6630. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6629. A Deep Dive Into Hailey Bieber’s Many, Many Face Masks

“Dealing with my issues one mask a time,” wrote Hailey Bieber beneath a recent Instagram carousel. While she’s not elaborating on said issues, her extensive collection of face masks have been exposed for every skincare obsessive’s over-analysis. Hailey Bieber has a face mask for every occasion and skin concern, it seems.

There she is, covered in mustard-yellow paste, slathered in a thick white cream, encased in a glossy lavender-grey treatment, and illuminated by the electric-blue glow of an LED device. There are hydrogel sheets, eye patches, and a rather arresting cobalt-blue mask from a recent trip to Seoul. Bieber is clearly not afraid to cast the net wide in pursuit of good skin.

Of course, we’ve long known Bieber as the reigning queen of glazed-donut skin. But beyond the perfectly dewy complexion and the seemingly endless supply of Rhode products, she’s a genuine skincare fanatic. And, someone who has been particularly candid about the challenges of maintaining her skin. Bieber has previously described her skin as dry, sensitive, and easily irritated, particularly by fragrances, harsh formulas, and certain sunscreens. She’s also spoken about her ongoing struggles with perioral dermatitis, an inflammatory condition that can cause uncomfortable redness, bumps, and flaking around the mouth and nose. Frequent travel, stress, hormonal fluctuations, and unfamiliar products can all contribute to her flare-ups.

As she’s previously explained, her approach when her skin is irritated is minimal: rinsing with water, using prescribed azelaic acid and clindamycin, hypochlorous acid, and Rhode’s ceramide-rich Glazing Milk. In her 2025 Beauty Secrets video, she also revealed that she generally skips a full morning cleanse in favor of a water rinse, saving the heavier-duty moisturizing for nighttime.

All of which explains a lot about her mask collection. Hydration, calming, barrier support, and a little depuffing appear to be the common threads. Although, importantly, a mask that hydrates dry skin won’t necessarily treat perioral dermatitis—and some formulas can aggravate it. So, what exactly is she using?

The first one I can immediately pinpoint is the bright-blue mask Bieber wore during her recent visit to South Korea: PYDERIN’s Hydrovuster PDRN SOS Hyal Soothing Mask. Sold largely through Korean pharmacies and dermatology clinics, it belongs to a new wave of PDRN-focused skincare products. PDRN, or polydeoxyribonucleotide, is derived from DNA fragments, commonly sourced from salmon, and has become a particularly buzzy ingredient in Korean regenerative skincare. The mask uses 10 forms of hyaluronic acid to attract and retain moisture, alongside ingredients such as panthenol, azulene, and barrier-supporting compounds. The distinctive blue tint comes from an azulene derivative, associated with soothing properties. The idea is to leave dehydrated, stressed skin feeling calmer, plumper, and more comfortable. It’s worth distinguishing topical PDRN from the injectable treatments offered in clinics, though: a sheet mask cannot promise the same regenerative results.

Then there’s Rhode’s Caffeine Reset Sculpting Cream Mask, which Bieber developed over approximately 18 months and more than 50 iterations. The rich, white rinse-off formula is designed as a morning pick-me-up for tired, puffy skin. “A cup of coffee for your face,” is what the Rhode copy says. Caffeine helps temporarily reduce the appearance of puffiness, while peptides, poppy extract, and phytosterols target radiance, surface hydration, and a firmer-looking complexion. Vanillyl butyl ether provides an invigorating sensation.

The brand’s other masking essential that I can spy in the IG carousel is the Peptide Eye Prep: cooling hydrogel under-eye patches. Formulated with caffeine, peptides, glycerin, and sodium PCA, they’re intended to hydrate the delicate under-eye area, temporarily minimize puffiness, and soften the appearance of fine lines. They are also super practical: Bieber has previously told Vogue Business that she wears hers to the gym or when heading out for coffee.

Hailey Bieber’s mask habit predates Rhode by several years. Among her earlier favorites are two treatments from Dr. Barbara Sturm. The original Face Mask combines aloe vera, chamomile, purslane, and kaolin clay for a combination of moisture, softness, and soothing care. Its Clarifying Mask, meanwhile, is more targeted towards blemish-prone skin, using zinc and kaolin to absorb excess sebum, alongside botanical ingredients intended to support the skin barrier. The latter is more of an occasional clarifying treatment than an everyday solution for reactive skin.

She’s also previously expressed her love for Drunk Elephant’s F-Balm Electrolyte Waterfacial, an overnight hydration treatment packed with humectants, squalane, niacinamide, and barrier-supporting lipids. It basically extends your nighttime mositurizing routine, as it helps the skin hold on to water while you sleep.

Her more recent masking repertoire also encapsulates the ongoing collagen obsession. One slide looks like Medicube’s PDRN Pink Collagen Gel Mask, a long-wear hydrogel treatment designed to boost hydration and give skin a visibly plumper finish. The brand’s Collagen Night Wrapping Mask offers a different experience: a liquid treatment that dries into a thin film, worn overnight to help retain moisture before being peeled or rinsed away in the morning. Despite the collagen branding, these are principally about surface hydration, softness, and the temporary appearance of bouncier skin, rather than replacing the collagen naturally found deeper in the skin.

And let’s not forget LOOPS’s Double Take Glow Mask, another Bieber-approved hydrogel treatment. This one brings together sunflower seed oil, aloe vera, and hyaluronic acid for a quick hit of hydration and radiance. With a suggested wear time of just 10 minutes, it’s the kind of mask you could don pre-makeup and a night out.

The assortment also includes treatments that are harder to identify from a selfie alone. The glossy, pale grey-blue mask pictured during what appears to be a professional facial resembles an alginate or rubberizing treatment, which is typically applied as a thick paste and allowed to set before removal. Such treatments can help retain moisture against the skin, although the exact benefits depend on their ingredients. The yellow and lavender-grey formulas remain mysteries for now.

Bieber’s carousel also features an LED light-therapy mask, another fixture of the increasingly high-tech celebrity skincare routine. Red and near-infrared light are commonly used to support collagen production and improve the appearance of fine lines and skin texture over time, while blue light is used for certain forms of acne. The precise device and light setting in Bieber's photograph aren’t clear (although we know her bestie Kendall loves her TheraFace Mask Glo), but the benefits of these treatments generally depend on consistency rather than a single session.

Bieber’s routine, of course, extends beyond what comes in a jar or compressed between plastic. She’s previously discussed PRP and PRF treatments, microneedling, and occasional laser sessions.

For anyone inspired to amp up their own mask collection, the important thing is to choose according to what your skin actually needs. Hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, and other hydrating ingredients make sense for tight, dehydrated skin; caffeine-based treatments can provide a temporary depuffing effect; and clarifying clay masks can be useful for excess oil, provided they don’t leave the skin feeling stripped. Apply hydrating sheet masks after cleansing and before moisturizer, unless the product directs otherwise. Cream masks generally need rinsing, while overnight wraps are designed to be the final step of an evening routine. Follow the recommended wear time: leaving a mask on longer doesn't automatically make it more effective. Introduce new formulas gradually, especially if your skin is reactive.

And while Bieber makes the case for having a mask for every occasion, those with active perioral dermatitis should be more selective. Heavy, occlusive products and unfamiliar ingredients can worsen the condition, and the best approach during a flare-up may be to forgo extra masking entirely in favor of a simple, dermatologist-guided routine.

Ultimately, the lesson from Hailey Bieber’s collection isn’t that you need eight different masks to achieve good skin. It’s that skincare is rarely one-size-fits-all, even for the woman who helped turn a glossy complexion into a billion-dollar beauty business.

#6628. Cozy Goes Chic This Winter

These UGG selects promise hot seasonal looks.

UGG boots have forever been a cold-weather favorite, and this season, they’re just the beginning of the brand’s cozy lineup. Between plush faux-fur jackets, soft vests for layering, and statement-making suede styles, there’s more than just booties to add to your winter wish list.

Think shaggy jackets with your favorite jeans, tall sheepskin boots to pull over leggings, and fuzzy vests that pair with everything from chunky sweaters to long-sleeve tees. With plenty of opportunities to play with proportions and textures, these are the pieces you’ll want to wear for morning coffee runs, weekend plans, and just about everything in between—all crafted with enduring quality to keep their shape and softness through countless winters.

Whether you’re treating yourself or shopping for someone on your gift list, there’s no shortage of cozy options to consider. Mix and match the eight styles below to find your favorite combinations for everything from casual weekend outfits to dressed-up holiday looks.

The Niah combines the brand’s signature plush UGGfluff fleece with classic toggle closures for a cozy extra layer that works with all your winter staples. Durable and easy to care for, it’s a go-to layering essential that pays for itself with everyday wear. Layer it over a fitted turtleneck with tailored trousers for a more polished outfit, or wear it with a chunky sweater, relaxed jeans, and Classic Ultra Tall boots on the weekend.

With its oversized, boxy fit and textural faux-fur mix, the Xyla brings plenty of dimension to a winter look. Expertly constructed from high-grade, resilient faux fur that resists matting, this statement piece doubles as a multi-season wardrobe investment. Keep the rest of your ’fit simple with your favorite jeans and a cozy knit, or pair it with a miniskirt, tights, and tall boots for a night out.

If you live in your Classic UGG boots all winter, the Classic Ultra Tall offers even more of that cozy, sheepskin-lined goodness you love. Reinforced stitching and a hard-wearing sole ensure it withstands daily cold-weather mileage year after year. For an extra-warm, casual weekend look, pair them with an oversized sweatshirt and long coat, finishing with a baseball cap and sunnies.

With plush sheepskin trim and fluffy seams that play up their cozy appeal, the Sunburst Tall boots would look right at home on an alpine getaway—but you don’t need a ski trip on the calendar to wear them. Soft faux fur, exaggerated shoulders, and a boxy fit give the Tesie a little more structure than your average fuzzy jacket, while toggle closures add a charming finishing touch. Wear it with leather pants and boots for dinner plans, or throw it over a knit dress and tights when you want to bundle up without hiding your outfit under a bulky coat.

For wintry days in the city, the Uptowner Tall boots bring together a chunky platform heel, grippy outsole, and soft sheepskin lining, so you can navigate slushy sidewalks without giving up a little height. Tough weather-defying materials mean they hold up to slick pavement while protecting your investment. They look great with a miniskirt, tights, and a chunky sweater, or with a knee-grazing dress and a tailored wool jacket for a more dressed-up occasion like dinner or drinks.

Play up the warmth with a knitted scarf and matching beanie for a snowy day, or keep things super easy for a weekend getaway by sporting an oversized sweatshirt and jeans tucked into the boots.

A little taller than the Classic Ultra Mini, but just as versatile, the Classic Mini II combines soft sheepskin with the familiar shape of UGG’s original boot. Pretreated against stains and moisture, it offers exceptional quality that outlasts the cold. Pair them with cuffed jeans and an oversized sweater on casual days, or straight-leg denim and a long wool coat when you want something a more timeless look.

#6627. Was This the Biggest Week in Sneakers of 2026?

As we inch towards the end of the year, there’s always a massive holiday rush in the sneaker industry (in addition to, well, everywhere else). Annual seasonal drops like the reliable Black Friday and Holiday XI launches from Jordan Brand, plus every major label trying to end the year on the highest note possible, make November and December some of the most exciting times to be a sneakerhead. To be fair, 2026 certainly still has some gas in the tank—plenty of us are already looking ahead to the return of the “Space Jam” Air Jordan 11 next month. Still, this week stands out even in an already crowded release calendar—in fact, I’m inclined to say it’s the biggest and best week of sneaker releases this year has had to offer so far.

Nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year. Reebok’s gradual revitalization takes a massive step in a fun, innovative new direction. And over at Converse, one of the most reliable celebrity designers in the footwear world is dropping some of his best work yet. Start drafting an apology letter to your credit card for everything you’re about to do with it—these are just a few highlights from the biggest, boldest week of sneakers in 2026 yet.

Who said anything about Samba fatigue? Turns out all it takes to make one of the most gen-pop shoes of the last decade feel brand new is a take like the one offered this week by Adidas Consortium collaborator Invincible, a Taiwanese brand that’s quickly establishing itself as a can’t-miss partner for the Three Stripes. Alongside a stellar line of apparel the brand has savvily outmaneuvered any semblance of cultural exhaustion with one of Adidas’s signature silhouettes by keeping it simple: They’ve outfitted the silhouette in a premium black unstructured leather and, bafflingly, a dress shoe sole rather than the Samba’s traditional gum rubber. With perforated Stripes and detailing that mimics those found on dressy leather brogues, it’s an instant contender for sneaker of the year…even if it just barely qualifies as one. This one goes on sale on November13, but with a catch—it’s an Asia exclusive. Pray to the resale market gods.

Nike has been struggling to find their next big-name collaborator, but in the meantime, some old favorites are still holding strong. One of those names is Union, the Los Angeles-based boutique founded by streetwear giant Chris Gibbs. This week, the brand is offering a buzzy iteration on the classic Nike Dunk that comes in a luxe brown suede and a heel-less mule silhouette. Like the Invincible Samba, the MO here is that all it takes to make an old shoe feel new again is a left-of-center take. These are dropping via SNKRS and Union on November 13, for $130 a pop.

Through Reebok’s ups and downs over the last decade, there has been one shining constant: Allen Iverson, the greatest athlete they’ve ever had on their roster. AI’s shoes are always in style, so if the brand simply brought back the original Question Mid silhouette for the shoe’s 30th anniversary, it’d be noteworthy enough. This year, though, they’ve taken the shoe to a new and fairly innovative space, refitting it with modern performance enhancements, making it court-worthy for the first time in decades. #6626. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6623. Inside Baby2Baby’s Star-Studded, Record-Breaking 15th Anniversary Gala

On Saturday evening at West Hollywood’s Pacific Design Center, Demi Moore asked a ballroom filled with Hollywood stars to take two deep breaths. The actress, who was being honored at Baby2Baby’s 15th anniversary gala, wanted everyone to consider the sense of relief that comes when a parent no longer has to worry about providing basic necessities for their child. It was one of the evening’s most moving moments, and a reminder of the mission behind a night that would go on to raise over $20 million dollars—the highest fundraising total for the nonprofit to date.

Presented by Paul Mitchell, the annual benefit drew a guest list that included Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau, Jessica Alba, Kerry Washington, Ciara, Chrissy Teigen, Paris Hilton, Sofía Vergara, Elsa Hosk, and Miranda Kerr, all gathering once more to celebrate the beloved organization.

Before the big night got underway, guests were treated to a luxe dining experience featuring 20 chefs and endless options. Jon Shook and Vinny Dotolo oversaw the hors d’oeuvres, which included tuna tartare and crispy rice with avocado, before attendees made their way to a dining area filled with stations from some of the most sought-after restaurants in Los Angeles and beyond. Carbone served its signature spicy rigatoni vodka, KazuNori rolled fresh hand rolls, Funke offered cannelloni bolognese, and Matū dished out Philly cheesesteaks en masse. Ensuring something for everyone, there were also oysters from Found Oyster, brisket from Moo’s Craft Barbecue, and crowd-pleasers by Mr. Chow, Holy Basil, and Saffy’s.

Once everyone settled in, Keke Palmer took the stage for opening remarks, bringing her comedic chops to the program while also speaking about her own experience as a mother. Between jokes, she emphasized the importance of ensuring that all parents have access to the fundamental basics. She then welcomed the Baby2Baby Angels—Alba, Washington, Ciara, and Teigen—who have supported the organization throughout its phenomenal growth.

For co-CEOs Kelly Sawyer Patricof and Norah Weinstein, the evening was an opportunity to reflect on just how much has changed since Baby2Baby’s early days. What began as a grassroots operation in Los Angeles has grown into a nationwide organization reaching 1.5 million children annually across all 50 states and distributing more than 850 million items over the past 15 years.

“We started from day one with our mission of providing basic essentials to children in need and knew we had a lot of work ahead of us,” Sawyer Patricof told Vogue. “We didn’t anticipate that our mission would naturally evolve into disaster relief because children living in poverty are the most vulnerable in every situation.”

The organization has now responded to more than 150 disasters nationwide, from the devastating Los Angeles wildfires to hurricanes in Florida and flooding in Texas. Another recent milestone came through its maternal health initiative. After piloting a program with the Biden administration to provide new mothers with critical supplies immediately after giving birth, Baby2Baby secured a $9 million investment from New York State last year.

The funding, Weinstein told Vogue, will provide Maternal Health & Newborn Supply Kits to 100,000 mothers giving birth on Medicaid across New York, along with millions of diapers for low-income families. “We lit up the Empire State Building in Baby2Baby green to celebrate this milestone,” she added, proudly.

Diaper access, however, remains at the center of Baby2Baby’s work. Over the years, the organization has successfully advocated for the elimination of sales tax on diapers in California and developed its own manufacturing system, allowing it to produce diapers for up to 80% less than average retail cost.

“Diaper need has been at the core of our mission, as nearly half of families in this country are struggling to afford them,” Weinstein and Sawyer Patricof noted. This year brought another major development with California’s first-in-the-nation Golden State Start program, which aims to provide 400 free Baby2Baby diapers to every newborn in the state through participating hospitals.

Back inside the ballroom, the evening’s lively fundraising efforts were already well underway. By the time Julie Bowen and Jenna Dewan stepped up to kick off the live auction, Baby2Baby had raised $7.5 million. Guests were encouraged to consider the huge impact of their donations: Every $1 million contribution will help to provide some 10 million diapers to children in need.

Andrew Garfield soon arrived on the podium to introduce Moore, who was presented with this year’s Giving Tree Award for her advocacy for children and families. A video montage featuring messages from Jon Hamm, Salma Hayek, Drew Barrymore, Jennifer Garner, and Moore’s daughters, among others, paid tribute to the actress before she addressed the room with a poignant speech. Moore reflected on motherhood and the importance of having a support system while raising children, pausing to look out to see her own daughters Rumer, Scout, and Tallulah Willis smiling back at her in the crowd.

With the most emotive moments behind them and a record-breaking fundraising target achieved, the crowd was ready to let loose. Katy Perry and Kelly Rowland introduced Cardi B, who sent the room wild with a performance of some of her most famous hits. Within moments, there wasn’t a person left sitting down as the ballroom turned into a full-fledged concert.

And the party didn’t stop there. Guests continued on to an after-party where DJ D-Nice kept the music going, while another round of food awaited anyone who had worked up an appetite. Burger She Wrote served late-night burgers, Chainsaw offered sweet treats, and Henry’s Secret Ice Cream and Leora rounded out the dessert offerings.

#6621. Upside-Down Cream Of Mushroom Tartlets

Upside-down tartlets went viral on social media, but they’re the party app we’re forever obsessed with. This hack uses store-bought puff pastry and transforms it into a beautiful, shareable snack filled with your sweet or savory filling of choice. Here, we’re leaning into cozy season by creating a cream of mushroom soup-inspired filling that pairs perfectly with the flaky pastry.

The mushrooms:You can find mushrooms used in two different ways here: both sliced and in a creamy, cheesy filling. The filling starts with a classic combination of minced mushrooms and shallots known as a duxelles (the very same mixture you can find at the base of a beef Wellington). To make this filling more mushroom soup-esque, we supplement it with Gùyere, heavy cream, and either sour cream or crème fraîche. The tangy dairy offsets some of the richness of the pastry while still containing enough fat to avoid curdling in the oven.

The pastry:When working with puff pastry, it’s important that you avoid prolonged exposure to heat. The dough is stacked with layers and layers of cold butter, which should melt and produce steam in the oven to create that signature flaky texture. Allowing that butter to melt while the dough sits on the counter will sacrifice that essential puff. If you notice your pastry start to warm up or stick to the counter, transfer it to a parchment-lined baking sheet, and let it cool down in the refrigerator for 10 to 15 minutes before you start working with it again.

Make ahead:The best part about this recipe is that you can make most of the components ahead of time. The mushroom filling can be made up to 3 days in advance, while the puff pastry squares can be cut and refrigerated up to a day before serving.

#6620. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6618. How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some issues we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process showed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Routine Excellence with Real Live Astronaut Reid Wiseman.”

#6617. Wendy's Is Making Major Changes To Its Menu—Including A Creamier Frosty

Wendy's is giving its classics an upgrade.

Wendy's is betting that better bacon and a creamier Frosty could help its sales slump. After reporting another decline in U.S. sales, the fast food chain is testing changes to several of its best-known menu items. This refresh will appear on the menu at some point in 2027, according to Fox News.

The most interesting update might be the Frosty, which Wendy's is working to make richer and creamier. The chain hasn't revealed the exact recipe changes, but given how recognizable the dessert has become, I'm curious how much the new version will differ. Whether or not it wins over fans who already know and love the original consistency is also up in the air.

Then there's the bacon. Wendy's is testing thicker, crispier bacon that could give sandwiches like the Baconator a more substantial bite. Personally, I think this is a pretty smart move. There's nothing more disappointing than ordering a bacon cheeseburger and barely noticing the bacon.

The chain is also experimenting with whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches and upgraded salads, all part of an effort to improve the quality of its existing menu rather than relying entirely on new products.

These changes aren’t coming out of nowhere. Wendy's reported a 5.7% decline in U.S. same-restaurant sales during the third quarter of 2026, marking another difficult period for the chain. In response, CEO Bob Wright is introducing a multi-year turnaround strategy called “Dave's Way,” named after Wendy's founder Dave Thomas.

The strategy focuses on improving the menu, marketing, restaurant operations, and digital ordering experience while giving customers better value for their money. But depending on your nearest location, it might come at a cost: breakfast.

Wendy's is allowing franchise operators to decide whether offering breakfast makes financial sense for their individual restaurants. That means some locations could stop serving breakfast altogether, although the company isn't eliminating the morning menu nationwide.

Wendy's also plans to simplify its offerings by removing lower-selling items that make restaurant kitchens more complicated to operate. However, the chain hasn't provided a complete list of products that could disappear.

The chain is still testing upgraded ingredients, so we won’t know the extent of the menu refresh or when it’ll roll out until some point in 2027. But if you’re anything like me, you’ll be waiting with bated breath to see how Wendy’s changes one of the most iconic fast food desserts.

#6616. 37 Family Dinner Ideas You’ll Make on Repeat

The good news about “family-friendly” dinners? They can be whatever you want them to be. Loaded sweet potato wedges eaten straight from the sheet pan? Absolutely. A dose of nostalgia by way of movie-night sloppy Joes, updated with a fiery kick of gochujang? No question about it. These are dinners for cautious eaters and adventurous ones alike—some familiar, some a little unexpected, and all worth bringing to the table.

Whether tonight calls for a cozy soup (that you can set and forget in your Instant Pot) or easy fish tacos (we have a hunch they’ll become part of your regular weeknight dinner rotation), we’ve got plenty of ideas to keep dinner interesting all year long.

Set tortillas, flaky cod or halibut, spicy lime sauce, and toppings out family-style and let everyone assemble their own piled-high tacos. It’s a simple weeknight family dinner that doubles as a choose-your-own-adventure activity.

Packed with ground chicken, white beans, and canned green chiles, this fast-cooking stew only gets better over time, so make a big batch. We promise, you won’t mind eating it two days in a row.

High-protein cottage cheese replaces often-pricier ricotta in this thrifty-ish spin on a familiar family favorite. More shocking: mozzarella is out too, in favor of tangy super-melter Fontina.

If your family loves pepperoni pizza, they’ll love this baked pasta, which hits all the saucy, spicy, cheesy notes with no takeout required. Roasting the sauce on a sheet pan concentrates its flavor before everything gets a blanket of cheese.

All the appeal of a spicy salmon roll, reassembled as a family-friendly bowl. Pickled cucumber and spicy mayo accompany crackly, broiled salmon cubes for a dinner that’s as fun to eat as it is easy to customize.

Smoky-sweet Korean gochujang lends a hum of heat to this riff on a childhood favorite. Soft buns and a stack of napkins do the rest.

Think chicken pot pie, but in cozy soup form. Complete with crackly, buttery shards of puff pastry you can tear and share, this family meal practically demands a crowd around the table.

This shareable skillet is packed with the flavors of a family-favorite appetizer, with roasted poblanos, red onions, and jalapeños smothered in cheesy sauce.

Store-bought pizza dough makes this family-friendly dinner a snap, even on busy weeknights. This California Pizza Kitchen-inspired recipe is smoky-sweet thanks to barbecue sauce, Gouda cheese, and frizzled mushrooms.

Store-bought zhug, a Yemeni-spiced cilantro sauce, and your broiler are the shortcuts to juicy, charred, baked chicken without a grill. It’s an easy, low-fuss dinner that delivers big flavor.

Somewhere between nachos and loaded potatoes, roasted sweet potatoes get topped with spiced ground beef and briny kimchi for a main dish that’s complete enough to enjoy straight off the sheet pan.

Genuinely juicy, supremely crispy, flavored like falafel, and browned in a skillet for ultimate ease. Serve them with your favorite burger toppings for an easy family dinner.

Sometimes you just want to cook an old faithful—the kind of dinner you know the whole family will love. That’s when you reach for this rich, cheesy, ever-reliable baked ziti.

These vibrant (and vegetarian) kale-and-black-bean-stuffed peppers are a repeat-worthy, one-dish dinner full of hearty flavor. Stirring a dollop of sour cream into the tomato sauce gives it rich texture.

Everyone loves a customizable dinner, and this shawarma-spiced chicken is made for it. Set out warm pitas and all your favorite fixings, like sliced tomatoes and cucumber spears, and let everyone build their perfect plate.

Shrimp cooked in garlicky, lemony butter is bound to be delicious. Serve it with crusty bread or toss it with pasta for a cozy weeknight meal the whole family will love.

Golden-edged tofu meets a bold, spicy satay-inspired peanut sauce in this quick, satisfying dish. Pile it over rice or serve with naan for scooping.

Canned pumpkin is good for way more than sweets. Here, lemon, Parmesan, and chile flakes turn it into a creamy, savory sauce that comes together while the pasta boils.

Spinach-packed dal is a lifesaver on nights when you’re strapped for time but craving something deeply comforting. Serve it with rice or flatbread for a quick vegetarian meal.

Tender soy-glazed chicken meatballs and crisp sesame green beans make a balanced family dinner that needs little else than a pot of rice.

Transform two favorite store-bought ingredients—cheese ravioli and crispy fried onions—into a rich and luscious skillet dinner with a crispy, savory top.

This sunny, dressed-for-summer family dinner relies on a pantry-friendly chicken marinade. All you need: sugar, vinegar, salt, and a few spices. Add couscous and dinner is done.

Make these succulent pork chops when it’s 6:26 p.m. on a Monday and you haven’t figured out what’s for dinner. The sweet-and-savory sauce makes this quick weeknight meal feel planned ahead.

Canned chickpeas and frozen broccoli keep this one-skillet dinner fast and thrifty, while cream cheese delivers on the faux pasta Alfredo front.

Leftover rice meets plenty of fresh ginger, soy sauce, and eggs in this satisfying 20-minute dinner. The key is starting with cold, cooked rice, which crisps up beautifully in a hot skillet.

Cherry tomatoes burst around a block of feta in the oven, forming a tangy, creamy pasta sauce. Calabrian chile paste brings a welcome kick that cuts through the richness.

This hearty catch-all skillet dinner tastes just as good in egg burritos the next morning, or make and freeze it up to three months ahead.

Upgrade grilled salmon with a punchy, vibrant dill chimichurri. It’s quick, fresh, and feels fancy enough to make you feel like you have your life together.

Much faster to make than risotto, this lemony, bright orzotto gets its herby savoriness from a pantry savior: store-bought jarred pesto.

Your favorite party dip, now in pasta form. Frozen spinach and jarred artichokes keep things convenient, while plenty of bubbling cheese makes this skillet dinner every bit as comforting as the original.

So tired you’re considering takeout? Try this simple, speedy stir-fry instead—it comes together in 25 minutes but tastes restaurant-quality.

Store-bought gnocchi bakes up crispy on the outside and pillowy on the inside, the perfect complement to browned spicy sausage and a sprinkle of finely grated Parmesan.

Give mac and cheese the hot wing treatment, because sometimes one comfort food just isn’t enough. It’s creamy, tangy, and just spicy enough to keep you coming back for another forkful.

Let your Instant Pot handle this warm, spicy, protein-packed, family-friendly dinner idea. Top it with a dollop of sour cream, a sprinkle of pickled onions, and whatever else floats your fancy.

Chicken and cabbage may sound pretty basic, but this stir-fry is anything but. Sambal oelek and fish sauce give it plenty of spicy, salty flavor, making it a nutritious family dinner that packs a punch.

Crisp bibb lettuce leaves make the perfect cups for this spicy larb-inspired chicken, which you can dress up with fresh herbs and fried shallots. It’s a fun, hands-on family dinner that gets everyone involved.

This is the kind of salad that can hold its own as a family dinner, packed with roasted sweet potato and tofu, crisp red apple, and a bright, herby green goddess dressing.

#6615. McDonald's Fans Are Celebrating The Return Of A Holiday Favorite They've Waited All Year For

McDonald's may be best known for its Big Mac burgers and mouthwatering fries, but that doesn't mean customers only frequent the chain for its classic menu items. In fact, fans are just as excited about some of the restaurant's seasonal offerings. Take its Holiday Pie, for instance. McDonald's introduced the limited-time dessert back in 1999, and it has consistently attracted customers for decades.

Like Mariah Carey thawing out for Christmas, McDonald’s Holiday Pie is finally back. The handheld dessert features creamy custard in a buttery crust, glazed with sugar, and topped with rainbow sprinkles.

The pie typically returns around November, although it's only available at select McDonald's restaurants. According to Allrecipes, fans have already spotted it in several cities this year, including New York, Philadelphia, and Boston, so if you're hoping to get your hands on one, your best bet is to check to see whether your local restaurant has it.

And the enthusiasm for this dessert is no joke. "Bruh they genuinely sold out in my area already," one fan commented on social media.

"Bro, this pie is delicious," another person wrote, while someone else had much bigger plans, sharing they’ll "probably eat 10 over the next two months!"

"Was hoping this was gonna return. Love the holiday pie," a different person commented. And someone else was already stocking up, writing, "I've ordered 2 yesterday and one was exactly sweet as I expected. Will try to get more before season time is done."

Of course, even a beloved holiday treat isn't immune to complaints about the price. During last year's release, one person wrote in a Reddit thread, "The holiday pie is my favorite, but pies are $2.89 here now and it's hard to justify spending $3 after tax on one." Another said their location had raised the price to $3.89 for a single pie.

Prices still vary by restaurant. For this year's return, one reviewer reported a price of $2.39 for one pie or $3.89 for two at their local Los Angeles McDonald's.

I guess you'll have to decide whether it's worth another taste of the holiday magic.

#6614. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.
